title: The Bronze at Eighteenth Street
premise: George Pullman installed a bronze of the 1812 battle beside his own door; a year later the army returned to Chicago, this time against his own striking workers. A walk about history, memory, and who gets to cast it in metal.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE BRONZE AT EIGHTEENTH STREET. A Monday afternoon in November 1904, at the intersection of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue.

Four stops around a single street corner. Beneath the pavement lies a battlefield; beside it stands a bronze that offers one interpretation of that battle; behind the bronze rises the mansion of the industrialist who financed it; and across the intersection looms the granite house that stared back at him. Every stop poses a question about what actually happened, and about who decided how it would be commemorated.

Begin where the street begins: on the ground where the battle was fought.

stops.text: Prairie Avenue at Eighteenth Street. Before the mansions, this was a landscape of sand hills along the lake. On 15 August 1812 the Battle of Fort Dearborn was fought across them, and the dead "lay in the sand, half buried where they were killed, until 1816". For more than a century an enormous cottonwood tree marked the site, although accounts disagree about its exact location. In 1900 a Tribune writer asserted that the Pullman house in front of this corner "stands about where the massacre took place". Now observe the street in 1904: brick, granite, gas lamps, and a schoolteacher escorting her class to see the sights. The battle is ninety-two years past, and it has been transformed into a lesson. The question is who composed that lesson. Walk east along Eighteenth Street to the bronze.

stage.caption: A teacher leads a line of schoolchildren along Eighteenth Street toward the monument.

stops.text: The monument. George Pullman commissioned it and installed it in 1893 near his own front door: Carl Rohl-Smith's bronze of the Potawatomi chief Black Partridge rescuing Margaret Helm, an officer's wife. It is theatrical and noble, and it may never have occurred. "Some historians regard the incident as the product of romantic imagination instead of eyewitness testimony", arguing that "Mrs. Helm rode her horse to the shore of Lake Michigan where she found refuge". The sculptor recruited his models at Fort Sheridan, among survivors of Wounded Knee, whom he described as "Indians of the most untamed sort", and one historian suggests the figures "may have owed more to Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West Show than to actual research". The teacher is reading the plaque aloud. Now consider the mansion this bronze stands guard over.

stage.caption: The teacher reads aloud to her class at the base of the monument while the children gaze up at the bronze.

stops.text: 1729 Prairie, the Pullman residence. The patron of the bronze manufactured railroad sleeping cars and constructed a company town south of the city, where his employees paid him rent. In 1894 he reduced their wages, but "he didn't reduce the rent in Pullman", and they went on strike. Here is the irony the bronze cannot convey: "a year after the statue's dedication", the Seventh Cavalry, the regiment of Little Big Horn and Wounded Knee, "came to Chicago to quell the Pullman riots of 1894". A regiment of the army whose wars the monument romanticizes arrived to suppress a strike against the man who had placed that battle at his doorstep. Pullman died of a heart attack in 1897, and the house will be demolished in 1922. Cross Prairie to the house that stared at his.

stage.caption: Two laborers carrying tools pause on the opposite sidewalk to study the Pullman house, then continue on their way.

stops.text: The Glessner corner, diagonally opposite Pullman's door. Pullman resented this house: "I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door". He spent his final years between the bronze and the granite. After his death, amid a string of notorious grave robberies and fears that former employees still sought revenge, his family buried him in a "lead-lined mahogany coffin, which was then sealed inside a block of concrete", beneath steel rails "bolted together at right angles". The historian Adam Selzer is candid about the legends: "Whether it's true or not, we don't really know". That uncertainty is the lesson of this corner: bronze, granite and concrete, and beneath all of it, the sand.

stage.caption: The class files past the Glessner corner on its way home, and the teacher glances back at the Pullman house.

legs.story: East along Eighteenth Street to the bronze beside the Pullman fence.
Back around the Pullman grounds to the façade of the mansion on Prairie Avenue.
Across the intersection to the Glessner corner, diagonally opposite Pullman's door.

endings.text: The walk ends here. In 1904 the bronze still stands at Eighteenth Street, narrating its story from a single perspective, even though several historians doubt the rescue it depicts ever took place. Pullman lies at Graceland beneath his concrete, the strike he crushed appears in every history of American labor, and the ground beneath this corner still contains the sand of 1812. A monument reveals who paid for it and what they wished to be remembered. Everything else, the historian must excavate.

keepsake.title: The Monument Question
keepsake.text: An interpretive card about the 1893 monument at Eighteenth Street and the contested history behind it; a reconstruction for this walk, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: The Battle of Fort Dearborn occurred in the area that is now the northern section of the street.

The dead of 15 August 1812 'lay in the sand, half buried where they were killed, until 1816'; the site, in the sand hills of the lake shore between 16th and 18th streets near the north-east corner of 18th and Prairie (accounts differ), 'was marked by for over a century by a large cottonwood tree'. A Tribune article of 1900 says the Pullman house 'stands about where the massacre took place'.
evidence.locator: The post's paragraphs on the site, its tree and the Tribune of 1900.

evidence.text: The Bronze at Eighteenth Street: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Bronze at Eighteenth Street: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

George Pullman commissioned Carl Rohl-Smith's bronze of the Potawatomi chief Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm, the wife of an army officer, placed in 1893 'near the intersection of Prairie Avenue and 18th Street'.
evidence.locator: The monument article's history; the cemetery post's paragraph on the 1893 statue, removed in 1931.

evidence.text: 'Some historians regard the incident as the product of romantic imagination instead of eyewitness testimony, stating that Margaret Helm was not the beneficiary of Black Partridge's dramatic rescue. In fact, before the battle turned into a massacre, Mrs. Helm rode her horse to the shore of Lake Michigan where she found refuge.'

Rohl-Smith obtained his models at Fort Sheridan, where he met survivors of Wounded Knee, whom he described as 'Indians of the most untamed sort'. His figures 'may have owed more to Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West Show than to actual research.'
In 1894 Pullman cut his workers' wages, but 'he didn't reduce the rent in Pullman', his company town; he 'died of a heart attack' on 19 October 1897.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on the strike and his death.

evidence.text: 'a year after the statue's dedication', the Seventh Cavalry, 'which had fought Indians so fiercely at Little Big Horn and Wounded Knee, came to Chicago to quell the Pullman riots of 1894.'

Pullman's firm raised Chicago buildings out of the mud 'on average six feet without causing them any damage'; his first sleeping car 'was finished in 1864'; Lincoln's body went home to Springfield in a sleeper while 'hundreds of thousands of people lined the route in homage'.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on building-raising, the sleeping car and Lincoln's funeral.

evidence.text: George M. Pullman Residence, 1729 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1922.
George Pullman, across the street, complained of the Glessner house: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'.

Fearing his body would be dug up, the family had him buried in a 'lead-lined mahogany coffin, which was then sealed inside a block of concrete', under steel rails 'bolted together at right angles', at Graceland Cemetery. An 1897 New York Times account gives a 'lead-lined box wrapped in tar paper' and 'an inch of asphaltum'; behind it, 'a lot of high-profile grave robberies lately' and the fear that 'some of the employees weren't quite done getting revenge'. The historian Adam Selzer: 'Whether it's true or not, we don't really know.'
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraph on the burial; the WTTW piece on the grave.

evidence.text: Glessner built at the corner of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue, diagonally opposite Pullman's mansion.
